opus-5.5.text:
I think what I enjoy most is the leverage, and I mean that in a very human sense. When I was a PhD student, and even before that, the joy came from getting my hands dirty: writing the code, debugging the robot at two in the morning, finally seeing a policy work on real hardware. That feeling is wonderful, and honestly I still miss it sometimes. But as an individual contributor, the scope of what you can explore is bounded by your own hours and your own ideas.

As a faculty member, I get to work with a group of really talented students, each bringing their own perspective and intuitions. A lot of the time the most exciting results in my lab come from directions I wouldn't have thought of myself. My job becomes less about solving one specific problem and more about asking good questions, shaping a research agenda, and creating an environment where students can take risks. When a student who came in unsure of themselves grows into someone with their own taste, who can define a problem and push it through, that's deeply satisfying in a way that a single paper never quite is.

The other thing I really value is the freedom to think long term. In robot learning, a lot of the important problems, like how robots can learn from human data at scale or how to get real generalization in manipulation, aren't things you solve in one project. Academia gives me room to pursue a coherent vision over many years, and to bet on directions that might not pay off right away.

That said, I try not to lose touch with the hands-on side completely. I still read code, I still go into the lab and look at what's happening on the robots, because I think you lose your intuition quickly if you're only looking at slides. So it's a balance, but the part I enjoy most is definitely seeing people grow and seeing ideas get much bigger than what I could have done alone.

r001.rationale: The response describes students expanding the lab’s ideas and helping pursue a long-term research vision, but does not clearly say they help realize Danfei Xu’s own vision.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it's the students. When I was an individual contributor, the thing I enjoyed most was the moment where you've been stuck on a problem for weeks and suddenly something clicks. As faculty, I still get that, but now I get it secondhand, many times over, through a whole group of people who are each going deep on something different. Watching a student go from "I have no idea why this isn't working" to confidently explaining to me why my suggestion was wrong is genuinely one of the best feelings in the job.

The other thing is breadth. As an IC you really have to pick a lane and go, because that's how you make progress. In a lab, I get to think about robot learning from several angles at once, like data collection, simulation, long-horizon planning, how we evaluate any of this, and I get to connect ideas across projects that no single person would have time to pursue alone. I'm less of a builder day to day, which I do miss sometimes, but I've become more of a connector and an editor, and that turns out to be its own kind of creative work.

And I'd add that teaching forces clarity. When you have to explain something to a room of students who haven't lived inside the field for years, you discover which parts you actually understand and which parts you've just gotten used to. That's uncomfortable in a good way, and it's made me a better researcher.

r001.rationale: The response says he enjoys seeing students make progress and connecting ideas across projects, but it does not say that others help realize his own vision.

astra-6.text:
What I enjoy most is working with students and watching them develop their own ideas. When you’re doing hands-on work, a lot of the satisfaction comes from solving a problem yourself. As faculty, you get to help someone find a direction, work through uncertainty, and eventually come back with something you wouldn’t have thought of. That’s really rewarding.

I also enjoy having room to think about how different projects connect—what bigger questions we should be asking. I still like the hands-on part, so there’s a balance. But helping students become independent researchers is probably the most exciting part for me.

r001.rationale: The response says Danfei enjoys helping students develop their own ideas and become independent researchers. It does not say he enjoys having others help realize his own vision.
